title: The Veto
objective: After this level you can explain how a veto works.
summary: A veto, Latin for "I forbid", is an executive's power to reject a bill. The US President has 10 days to sign or veto; Congress can override by two-thirds. Override rules vary by country.

cards.headline: "Veto" is Latin for two words: "I forbid."
cards.body: In ancient Rome it was the term for a protest by a tribune of the people against a measure of the Senate or the magistrates. Presidents today still use the same word to stop a bill in its tracks. How much power does that give them?

cards.headline: Sign it or send it back
cards.body: A veto is an executive's power to reject a bill, preventing it from becoming law. In the US, the President has 10 days (Sundays excepted) to sign a bill or return it to Congress with objections. Congress can override a veto, but only by a two-thirds vote in each chamber. And if Congress adjourns so the President can't return the bill, it's a pocket veto, which can't be overridden at all.

cards.fact: Franklin D. Roosevelt vetoed 635 bills. Congress overrode 9.
cards.context: That's more vetoes than any other US president. Two-thirds of both chambers is a lot of agreement to find, and FDR's record shows it: nine overrides out of 635 tries.

cards.headline: Different countries, different bars
cards.body: Override rules vary. Two-thirds is most common, in countries such as Mexico, Ghana and the Philippines. Poland needs three-fifths; Brazil needs only an absolute majority in both chambers. International IDEA points out what a veto really does: if the president backs a bill, an ordinary majority passes it. If the president opposes it, lawmakers need a supermajority.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing about vetoes: they change how many votes a bill needs to pass.

cards.headline: Veto: explained
learned: The US President has 10 days to sign or veto
Congress overrides by two-thirds of each chamber
Override bars vary from country to country

questions.prompt: The word "veto" comes from Latin. What does it mean?

options.label: I delay
options.rationale: It's stronger than a delay: "I forbid."

questions.explanation: Veto is Latin for "I forbid", the term for a Roman tribune's protest.

questions.prompt: According to International IDEA, how does a veto change the majority a bill needs?

options.label: Every bill then needs a unanimous vote
options.rationale: Overrides need a supermajority, not everyone.

options.label: A bill the president opposes needs a supermajority
A bill the president supports needs a supermajority
options.rationale: With the president's support, an ordinary majority is enough.

options.label: It makes no difference to the numbers
options.rationale: It changes the bar from ordinary to supermajority.

questions.explanation: With the president's support an ordinary majority passes a bill; against a veto, lawmakers need a supermajority.

questions.prompt: A US bill has passed the House and the Senate in identical form. What can still stop it becoming law?

options.label: A presidential veto that Congress fails to override
A second reading in the House of Lords
options.rationale: That's the UK Parliament, not Congress.

options.label: A vote by the Supreme Court before signing
options.rationale: The next step is the President, not a court.

options.label: Nothing: it becomes law automatically
options.rationale: It still goes to the President, who can veto it.

questions.explanation: After both chambers pass identical text, the bill goes to the President, who can veto it; Congress can override only by two-thirds of each chamber.
